body.text: In short:
Councils across Sydney are clamping down on the use of smart glasses in public places, including at popular beaches.
Waverley Council, which manages many of Sydney's eastern suburbs beaches, has approved a ban of the technology in principle.
NSW Premier Chris Minns says he will consider whether statewide action can be taken.
Smart glasses could be banned on some of Australia's most popular beaches this summer, as local councils crack down on the emerging technology.
A recent study by the University of Sydney, which looked at 350 videos posted online that were filmed using smart glasses, found 60 per cent contained potential harassment.
One of the primary concerns is the filming of women in so-called "rizz videos", in which the wearer attempts to flirt with strangers.
Waverley Council, which manages many of Sydney's eastern suburbs beaches, including Bondi, Bronte and Tamarama, has approved a ban in principle of the technology, and is consulting on enforcement.
Bondi Ward councillor Michelle Stephenson said public safety was a top priority.

"Bondi is a beach where people come to swim, they come to exercise, they bring their children, they're in public spaces, they're in and out of change rooms. We need to know that they are being taken care of," Cr Stephenson said.
Waverley Council Mayor Steven Lewis added it was important to "consider how best to protect the privacy of residents and visitors".

Randwick City Council, which covers Coogee and Maroubra, is currently investigating expanding its ban on the glasses at public pools to cover those beaches, while Northern Beaches Council, which manages beaches from Manly to Palm Beach, is considering a similar move.

"Council runs a lot of places where if people are using covert recording devices, it creates a huge potential for personal safety and child protection issues to arise," Northern Beaches councillor Kristyn Glanville said.
Sydney's Inner West Council on Tuesday night became the latest local government to ban the use of smart glasses at council-run swimming and recreation facilities.

"Our key area of concern is that we would have a resident in a change room or in a swimming pool area, that they're recorded and this is broadcast onto the internet, onto social media and their rights are infringed on in terms of privacy," councillor Kerrie Fergusson said.

In Sydney, the City of Sydney, Canterbury-Bankstown, North Sydney, Mosman, Blacktown and Sutherland Shire councils have all introduced bans at public pools, mostly with exceptions for people with disabilities.
Regional areas are also moving towards their own bans as the weather warms.
"It's been pushed upon us and it's been without any real due diligence on the impacts of, you know, people's privacy in particular," Bellingen Shire councillor Dominic King said.
NSW premier to consider action
The federal government faced pressure from the crossbench to include specific regulations for smart glasses in its draft privacy policy, released in August, but decided against doing so.

"The Privacy Act consultation does not go to issues of import restrictions; however, we are not ruling anything out in terms of other measures we can take," Attorney-General Michelle Rowland said at the time.
"I would like other councils to consider what kind of public areas they have in their sphere of influence where this could apply."
When asked on Wednesday morning, NSW Premier Chris Minns said he would consider whether statewide action could be taken.
"I haven't really thought about it but I'll look at [councils'] initiatives and see if they're appropriate statewide," Mr Minns said.
Rules need to 'keep up with the times'
At Sydney's Bronte Beach, Freya Lundberg believed smart glasses should not be allowed at the beach.
“They can record people, right? So that doesn't feel too safe for me, especially as a woman," she said.
"Phones are there, people could record me technically yes, but if it feels more discreet when it's in glasses, so I would prefer not to have that."
Bellingen resident Emma Lawson said she agreed with the council's consideration of smart glasses.
"I definitely think that there needs to be regulations around beach areas, or swimming pools, even in childcare as well," she said.
"Overall, with AI and everything like that … we need to have rules that develop with it and keep up with the times."
Her partner Josh Foster said it was important for people in public spaces to feel safe.
Peter Kemp shared a similar sentiment.
"I think it's a good move if people are going to be using smart glasses and I guess invading people's privacy," he said.

"But smart glasses I believe do offer a terrific benefit for certain individuals. And it may be that people who have difficult seeing and understanding the environment that they're in can use and record what they see.
"And also tourists visiting different locations and want to capture that memory. But in change rooms, swimming pools, the beach, I don't think it's appropriate."
